item.title: Atmospheric River Season for the Pacific Northwest | NASA Earthdata
item.summary: Atmospheric rivers periodically bring heavy surf, rain, strong winds, and flooding potential to the Pacific Northwest coast of the United States ...
item.page_text:
Atmospheric rivers periodically bring heavy surf, rain, strong winds, and flooding potential to the Pacific Northwest coast of the United States and western Canada. These long columns of warm, moisture-laden air originate over the ocean in subtropical regions. Because the atmospheric rivers that hit North America tend to originate near Hawaii, they are colloquially called a "pineapple express." When these rivers of wet air reach the West Coast, they often drop substantial amounts of rain and snow.
The true-color corrected reflectance image above from the VIIRS instrument aboard the NOAA-20 platform shows a swirling, comma-shaped band of clouds approaching the coast on November 12, 2026.
Press play in the lower left corner of this animation to see back-to-back atmospheric rivers approaching the U.S. and Canadian coasts. Rain and snow estimates come from the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) (IMERG) algorithm, which combines passive-microwave observations from the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) constellation of satellites, infrared observations from geosynchronous satellites, and calibration data derived from rain gauges. The data show the IMERG precipitation rate at 30-minute intervals from 00:00 UTC on November 11 to 15:00 UTC on November 13.
